ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory enhanced due diligence screening of all UBOs (25% threshold), directors, officers, authorized signatories, and material franchise counterparties against the Global Affairs Canada Consolidated Canadian Autonomous Sanctions List (under the Special Economic Measures Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act), the United Nations Security Council consolidated sanctions list, the Criminal Code 'listed terrorist entities' register (s. 83.05), and the OFAC SDN List as best practice for USD-denominated payment rails. All subjects must also be screened for domestic and foreign politically exposed persons (PEP) status per FINTRAC guidance; automated screening results and source documents must be retained in the corporate AML/CFT due diligence file.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: BC Corporate Online (BC Registry Services, Ministry of Finance) at https://www.bcregistry.gov.bc.ca, for a provincial British Columbia Business Corporation; alternatively, the Corporations Canada NUANS online portal if a federal CBCA entity is elected
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under the British Columbia Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c. 57, and the Business Corporations Act General Regulation, BC Reg 104/2004, the corporate legal name must be composed of letters of the English alphabet and/or numerals, or a combination; Chinese characters are not permitted in the registered corporate name. A romanized Pinyin transliteration (e.g., 'MALATANG') is therefore mandatory, together with a distinctive element and a prescribed legal element (e.g., 'XXX Malatang Restaurant (Canada) Ltd.'). The name must satisfy the statutory distinctiveness test and must not be confusingly similar to an existing BC-registered corporate name, extraprovincial name, or registered trademark.

Lawyer, Barrister, Solicitor, Notary, Auditor, Architect, Engineer

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If BC Registry rejects or conditions a name request, the applicant may file a formal Reconsideration application with BC Registry Services within 30 days of the rejection, attaching a fresh name search, comparative evidence, consent letters, and written legal argument. A name approval may be renewed for one further 56-day period before expiry. If the Registrar confirms the refusal, an aggrieved person may seek judicial review before the Supreme Court of British Columbia under the Judicial Review Procedure Act, RSBC 1996, c. 241, within 30 days of the decision. For a federal CBCA name refusal, a written NUANS reconsideration must be filed with Corporations Canada within 60 days.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual or registered-agent office is permissible for the statutory registered office and records office only, provided the address is a physical street address in British Columbia (not a post office box), is open during regular business hours, and is capable of accepting service of process under the British Columbia Business Corporations Act. However, the fast-casual self-serve broth-bowl franchise must maintain real commercial substance: a licensed physical food-premises location under the Public Health Act, SBC 2008, c. 28, and the provincial Food Premises Regulation, plus a valid municipal business licence, federal GST/HST registration, and, once operational, WorkSafeBC and merchant-acquirer registration. A virtual address cannot satisfy those operational and regulatory requirements.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Registered office and records address: low risk (less than 5% probability of unannounced inspection per annum). Operating restaurant premises: high risk (approximately 90% or greater probability of at least one unannounced public-health food-premises inspection within the first operating year, with statutory re-inspection follow-ups), because British Columbia health authorities and municipal inspectors hold statutory rights of entry at any reasonable time, supplemented by routine WorkSafeBC and municipal business-licence compliance visits.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c 57, as amended; ss 10(1) (incorporation), 24 (authorized share structure), 48 (Notice of Articles), 51 (incorporation application), 108 (first directors).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Corporate Registry, BC Registries and Online Services, Ministry of Finance, Province of British Columbia
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Incorporation Application and Notice of Articles (Form 1) filed electronically via BC Corporate Online
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital under the BC Business Corporations Act. Shares may be issued for a stated value without an initial escrow deposit for a private corporation; an escrow account is required only for certain public interest or exempt-market issuances.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED: That the Corporation accepts the subscriber’s subscription for one common share, par value none, at a price of CAD 1.00, and the Chief Financial Officer is authorized to issue and deliver such share upon payment. FURTHER RESOLVED: That the registered office of the Corporation be established at the address set forth in the Notice of Articles in British Columbia, and that the consent of the office holder is received. FURTHER RESOLVED: That [Name] be appointed President, [Name] be appointed Secretary, and [Name] be appointed Treasurer, each to serve until the next annual general meeting or until successors are elected. FURTHER RESOLVED: That all banking authorities be established such that two signatures are required for transactions exceeding CAD 10,000.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registries and Online Services – Name Request Portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Search desired corporate name using the BC Corporate Online name request service, review corporate name availability, submit a Name Request with a proposed name or rely on the existing NUANS name search report; pay the applicable name reservation fee.
required_dossiers: Name search report or NUANS search result
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the reserved name is refused, file a statement of objection or submit a revised name through the same portal, or apply for a name reconsideration by the Director.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Incorporation Application and Notice of Articles Filing
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registries and Online Services – BC Corporate Online portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete the online incorporation application, attach the Articles, provide the registered office address, the first directors and their consents, and authorize the filing of the Notice of Articles; pay the filing fee and obtain the Certificate of Incorporation.
required_dossiers: Form 1 – Incorporation Application and Notice of Articles
Registered office address and consent of the office holder
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried, correct the particular deficiency in the BC Corporate Online portal and resubmit within 14 days; if the query concerns the name, refile with a revised name.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Business Number Registration and Tax Account Setup
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) – Business Registration Online
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After receiving the Certificate of Incorporation, register with the CRA for a Business Number, GST/HST account (if applicable), payroll account, and corporate income tax account, using the BC incorporation information and the assigned corporate registry number.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the CRA issues a formal notice or rejects the registration, review the corporate information in the Business Registration Online and request correction through CRA Business Enquiries; provide supporting corporate records.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Issuance of Shares and Corporate Record Establishment
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporate Secretary (internal governance) with Registered Agent filing support
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Execute share certificates, register the shareholders in the share register, maintain the register of directors and officers, adopt the minute book, and record the registered office and records office; submit any required post-incorporation filings to BC Registry if the initial Notice of Articles changes.
required_dossiers: Consent of each director and officer
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If share issuance is challenged, call a special board meeting and approve a curative resolution, issue corrected certificates, and file a notice of change with BC Registry if necessary.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registries and Online Services – Certified Copy Request
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Order certified copies of the Certificate of Incorporation, Notice of Articles, and Articles from BC Registries to be used for municipal licensing, banking, and land or lease applications; verify the package contains the corporate number and legal name.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the registry service delays, contact BC Registries customer service or escalate through the online chat; reorder certified copies if the initial package was incomplete.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Environmental Health Department of the local health authority (e.g., Vancouver Coastal Health or Fraser Health) and the municipal Licensing and Building Department
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Business Licence and Food Service Establishment Permit

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: British Columbia Ministry of Environment and Climate Change Strategy (BC ENV), Environmental Assessment Office
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Registration category, not full EIA, for a small-scale food preparation operation with expected low contaminant discharge
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Wastewater must comply with the municipal sewer use bylaw and any facility-specific Sewer Use Permit; grease interceptors must be installed and maintained to limit grease and solids discharges; ventilation exhaust VOC limits are governed by regional district or municipal air quality bylaws; food waste disposal shall be directed to licensed organic waste or solid waste facilities with no discharge to storm drains.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety inspection and Fire Safety Plan approval are required under the BC Fire Code; a structural load inspection and building occupancy clearance must be obtained from the municipal building authority; WorkSafeBC registration and occupational health and safety clearance for food service equipment operation, electrical safety, slips/trips and ergonomic hazards are required before opening to the public.

Bill of Lading (ocean/air/rail/road) evidencing movement of goods out of Canada
Inward Remittance Certificate or bank confirmation evidencing receipt of export proceeds

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada; prudential regulation by Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI); AML/CFT supervision by Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC); trade sanctions administered by Global Affairs Canada
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada has full current and capital account convertibility under IMF Article VIII and maintains no exchange controls. Capital contributions, profit repatriation, royalty payments, and loan repayments do not require central bank approval. The Canadian dollar is freely convertible, including against USD and offshore CNY. Remittance is subject to Part XIII non-resident withholding tax where applicable and to FINTRAC transfer reporting thresholds, but not to exchange-control rationing or convertibility limits.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no statutory export-proceeds surrender timeline, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no requirement to repatriate export receipts into a designated domestic account. Foreign currency may be retained in a Canadian Schedule I bank multi-currency account. All international electronic funds transfers of CAD 10,000 or more are reportable to FINTRAC, and supporting underlying commercial documentation must be retained for verification.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low-to-medium viability as a primary treasury rail for a Canadian operating corporation. Offshore electronic money institutions (EMIs) are not authorized banks under the Bank Act and cannot accept deposits or hold escrowed corporate funds in Canada. They may operate as money services businesses only if registered with FINTRAC, and retail payment activities require registration under OSFI-administered Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA). A foreign EMI can act as a payment facilitation layer for point-of-sale receipts or international vendor payments, but the primary capital escrow and operational liquidity accounts must sit with a Canadian regulated financial institution.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Canadian law does not impose an absolute mandate for physical director attendance when opening a corporate bank account, but regulated institutions retain discretion to require it. For foreign-controlled BC corporations, Schedule I banks generally accept a remote opening if directors complete FINTRAC-compliant video identification and provide notarized passports, corporate extracts, and beneficial ownership declarations. In practice, a physical meeting at a BC branch with a director or authorized officer is recommended for capital escrow accounts and for foreign jurisdiction entities with complex ownership.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Opaque beneficial ownership chain with overseas Chinese or multi-tiered holding entities
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Notarized passports and utility bills for all directors and ultimate beneficial owners; registry extracts of every intermediate entity; share register and corporate resolutions; trust deed documenting any nominee or trust layer; credible source-of-funds evidence; customer due diligence questionnaire from the remitting foreign bank.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unexplained inbound wires from high-risk or non-treaty jurisdictions
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Master licence agreement; shareholder subscription or loan agreement; board resolutions authorizing the capital contribution; invoice schedule for licence and franchise fees; remitter bank statement confirming commercial origin; explanation of payment rails; sanctions and PEP screening results; independent corporate regulatory history report.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions, PEP, or adverse media hit on a director or shareholder
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Global Affairs Canada and UN sanctions screening reports; OFAC-comparable country check documentation; detailed PEP relationship explanation; source-of-wealth and source-of-funds report; independent legal opinion on sanctions exposure; evidence that no prohibited party receives royalties or distribution proceeds.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Perceived mischaracterization of franchise royalty payments as cost reimbursement or dividend
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Revenue Canada-compliant master licence agreement; trademark and IP registration certificates; OECD transfer pricing documentation; detailed calculation of the 4% to 8% royalty pool; BC business licence and municipal operating permits; audited financial statements; Part XIII withholding tax remittance records or applicable treaty rate certificate.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Mismatch between BC registered office, operational restaurant site, and treasury account address
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Lease agreement for each restaurant location; utility statements; municipal business licence; floor plan and health inspection record; corporate annual report confirming registered agent; letter of explanation from corporate counsel; resolution authorizing separate treasury registered office for liquidity management.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound capital injections from foreign shareholders must be routed via compliant SWIFT MT103 or MT202 to a Canadian Schedule I bank account opened in the legal name of CA_CORP. The wire must state clear purpose text such as 'equity subscription' or 'shareholder capital contribution' and the beneficiary account must match the corporate registry name. Canadian banks require the corporate legal name, BC registration number, business number, and beneficial ownership declaration. The receiving bank verifies the source of funds and files a FINTRAC EFT report for transactions of CAD 10,000 or more. No Bank of Canada exchange-control approval is required. Equity subscriptions are generally not subject to Canadian withholding tax; shareholder loans must have written loan agreements and corporate resolutions to establish arm's-length terms and Part XIII treatment of any interest.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound cross-border disbursements for franchise inventory, equipment, lease royalties, and licensor fees should use SWIFT MT103 creditor-side transfers, with MT103 narrative containing contract or master licence references. For supplier trade flows, ICC UCP600-compliant commercial letters of credit may be issued through the Canadian issuing bank with SWIFT MT700/MT710 documentation. Domestic payroll and supplier payments should clear via Canada's Large Value Transfer System (LVTS) or Real-Time Rail (RTR) when enabled. Royalty and management fee wires must include underlying tax documentation, gross-up calculation, and a reference to the applicable Canada-China income tax treaty if treaty benefits are claimed. All outgoing transfers above prescribed thresholds are automatically reported to FINTRAC, and the corporate treasury file must retain bank confirmation, board resolution, invoice, and counterparty KYB records.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Plain vanilla deliverable CAD/USD forward contracts
Non-deliverable forwards on CNH/USD for Chinese yuan settlement exposure where CAD/CNH deliverability is thin

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No mandatory audit for a non-listed private corporation solely on revenue or asset thresholds; audit is required if the company is a reporting issuer, subject to a shareholder resolution requiring an audit, or carrying on a regulated activity. Private BC shareholders may waive the auditor appointment by unanimous consent.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS for publicly accountable enterprises; private corporations may apply Canadian ASPE or IFRS consistently.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Before filing the annual report, the board must confirm the register of members reflects all share transfers and must record any individual holding 25% or more of voting rights or control in fact. Corrections are made in the minute book and any applicable persons-with-significant-control register; no separate UBO filing is submitted with the BC annual report except where BC land-ownership transparency obligations apply.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book (shareholder meetings, board meetings and resolutions)
Register of Individuals with Significant Control (if prescribed or land-ownership trigger applies)

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 27.0% combined federal and British Columbia general corporate income tax (15% federal + 12% BC); eligible Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) pay a combined 11% on the first CAD 500,000 of qualifying active business income (9% federal + 2% BC).
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No statutory corporate tax holiday is currently available in respect of this entity type. The principal preferential feature is the federal Small Business Deduction and the BC small-business tax rate applicable to CCPCs, which lowers the combined effective tax rate from 27% to 11% on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income. Federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) credits, investment tax credits, accelerated capital cost allowance, and manufacturing or processing incentives may apply if the corporation has qualifying expenditures. A franchise/IP licensing entity earning royalty income may not qualify for the small-business rate unless the income is actively carried on in Canada and the corporation is a CCPC under applicable statutory rules.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Form T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, filed electronically via CRA-certified software through the CRA EFILE/NetFile system. Due to Canada's single-administration agreement, the T2 serves as both the federal return and the British Columbia provincial corporate income tax return.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T2 must be filed within 6 months after the corporation's taxation year-end. The final income tax balance is due within 2 months after the taxation year-end for a non-CCPC, or within 3 months after the year-end for an eligible CCPC claiming the small business deduction. Corporations with annual taxable income above prescribed thresholds are required to pay monthly instalments.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 1, Line 10 — Net income before adjustments
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Start with accounting net income from the corporation's financial statements, then apply tax adjustments for items such as amortization, reserves, dividends received, interest deductibility limits, and non-deductible expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A Canadian-incorporated corporation is treated as resident in Canada even if controlled by non-residents; therefore all worldwide income must be reported. The non-resident ownership percentage does not alter the return except for applicable treaty withholding on distributions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Apply available deductions such as non-capital loss carryovers, capital cost allowance, and deferred income amounts to determine taxable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Taxable income is computed identically for a non-resident-owned Canadian corporation; there is no territorial exemption for income earned inside Canada. Foreign-source business income may be eligible for treaty-based relief or foreign tax credits.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculate and apply non-capital losses from prior years (subject to the 20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback rules) against taxable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident owned corporations may only utilize losses that arose in Canada and that are traceable to Canadian-source business income; losses of foreign parent affiliates are not deductible.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 23, GRIP account — General Rate Income Pool
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tracks the amount of taxable income taxed at the general rate that can be designated as eligible dividends, affecting the amount of withholding tax payable by non-resident shareholders.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a CCPC controlled by Chinese residents, maintaining a GRIP balance is essential to qualify for the lower 5% withholding rate on dividends to a corporate shareholder resident in China under the Canada-China tax treaty.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 12 / BC provincial calculation — Provincial tax payable
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculate the British Columbia tax after applying the BC general rate, the BC small business rate, and any BC tax credits. This schedule is embedded in the T2 calculation process.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the corporation has a permanent establishment in British Columbia, a provincial income allocation schedule must be completed; non-resident shareholders do not execute this schedule personally, but the corporation must report BC-source income allocations accurately.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing of the T2 attracts a penalty of 5% of the unpaid balance of tax, plus 1% of the unpaid balance for each full month the return is late, up to a maximum of 12 months. A second offence within a three-year period raises the penalty to 10% plus 2% per month, up to a maximum of 20 months. Interest accrues daily at the CRA prescribed rate on the unpaid balance. The gross-negligence penalty for a false statement or omission is 50% of the understated tax. Failure to file a T106 or required information return carries a separate daily penalty of CAD 100 per day, up to CAD 2,500, and further penalties may be imposed for wilful default.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% under subsection 212(2) of the Income Tax Act, applied by the Canadian company to dividends paid or credited to non-residents, unless reduced under an applicable tax treaty.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke a treaty reduction, the beneficial owner must provide the payer with an annual Certificate of Residence issued by the foreign tax authority (e.g., the State Taxation Administration of China) evidencing residency in the treaty country. The Canadian payer must complete and submit Form NR301 (or NR302 for a corporate shareholder claiming the 5% treaty rate) to the CRA, retain a copy of the certificate on file, and apply the reduced rate at the time of payment. If the required forms and certificate are not received before the payment is made, the payer must withhold at the statutory 25% rate; a refund of the excess withholding can be claimed by the non-resident via a T2 filing or by filing Form T503.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Part XIII withholding on royalties paid to non-residents is 25%. Interest paid to arm's-length non-residents is generally exempt from withholding tax, but interest paid to non-arm's-length shareholders is subject to the 25% statutory rate unless reduced by treaty. Under the Canada-China double tax agreement, the treaty rate is generally 10% for royalties and 10% for interest, and dividends are capped at 15%, with a reduced 5% rate available to a beneficial owner that is a company owning at least 10% of the voting shares (subject to the treaty's title or anti-abuse provisions).

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1,000,000 in aggregate reportable non-arm's-length cross-border transactions with a single non-resident related party triggers the requirement to file Form T106 (Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents). There is no fixed statutory monetary threshold for the preparation of a separate Local File or Master File in Canada; however, CRA's contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation standard expects the taxpayer to prepare a functional analysis, a comparability analysis, and a selection of the most appropriate method before filing the T2. Multinational groups with consolidated revenue equal to or exceeding EUR 750 million are separately required to file a Country-by-Country report.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not administer jurisdiction-specific 'Economic Substance Regulations' of the type introduced in offshore financial centres. Instead, the Income Tax Act's General Anti-Avoidance Rule (s. 245), the sham doctrine, and substance-over-form principles allow the CRA to recharacterize a transaction or disregard an entity that lacks genuine economic substance. A BC corporation engaged in cross-border royalty or franchise licensing must maintain a real presence in British Columbia, including active business records, local board meetings, and substantive decision-making, to prevent an attack on its Canadian tax residence or treaty eligibility.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion — wilful concealment of revenue
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberate understatement of royalty receipts or franchise fees from related/non-related Chinese master franchisees, failure to invoice cash-paid broth-bowl store receipts, or suppression of POS records to reduce corporate income tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Criminal prosecution under subsection 239(1) of the Income Tax Act: upon conviction, a fine of not less than 50% and not more than 100% of the tax evaded, plus imprisonment for a term of up to 5 years. Civil gross-negligence penalties of 50% of the understated tax plus interest may also be assessed.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who participate in, authorize, or acquiesce to the concealment may be charged jointly with the corporation. The corporate veil is pierced in cases of fraud; directors face personal civil restitution, criminal fines, incarceration, and the possibility of travel bans as a condition of bail or a criminal restraint order.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Maintaining a BC business corporation with no real office, no active board, no Canadian employees, and no commercial substance, while channelling Canadian franchise royalty income into a related Hong Kong or Cayman entity to avoid BC corporate tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may invoke section 245 of the Income Tax Act to deny the tax benefit; reassess the foreign entity as the taxable Canadian agent; and impose gross-negligence penalties of 50% of the additional tax. A sham finding can also invalidate inter-company contracts and trigger penalties under subsection 238(1) for failing to file a return.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly permit the corporation to operate as a shell may lose the limited-liability protection. They are jointly and severally liable for the corporation's unpaid GST/HST and payroll source deductions under section 323 of the Excise Tax Act and section 227.1 of the Income Tax Act, respectively. In serious fraud cases, they may also face director liability orders and travel bans.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Setting the royalty or management fee charged to the related Chinese master franchisee at an artificially low rate, or paying an above-market deductible royalty to a related IP-holding corporation in a zero-tax jurisdiction, thereby shifting profits out of British Columbia.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Canada Transfer Pricing rules under section 247 permit the CRA to adjust cross-border non-arm's-length amounts to arm's-length terms. A penalty equal to 10% of the net transfer-pricing adjustment is exigible unless the taxpayer can demonstrate reasonable efforts to determine and apply an arm's-length price. Interest runs from the original reassessment date, and treaty benefits can be denied under the Limitation of Benefits provisions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who authorize fraudulent inter-company pricing may be held personally liable for the aggregate penalty under section 247 and interest. In criminal cases, the director can be named as a party to the offence, leading to imprisonment and a personal fine equal to the unpaid tax.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately structuring cross-border royalty telegraphic transfers to avoid reporting thresholds, accepting payments through unregistered third-party deposit accounts, or failing to maintain beneficial-ownership records of the Chinese shareholders controlling the BC corporation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: If the corporation is a reporting entity under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, penalties can reach CAD 2,000,000 per administrative violation for failing to implement the AML program, report large cash/large virtual-currency transactions, or maintain beneficial-ownership records. Non-reporting entities remain subject to criminal charges where the conduct is part of a tax evasion scheme.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be prosecuted for money-laundering offences under section 462.31 of the Criminal Code of Canada if they knowingly laundered proceeds of tax evasion. Conviction carries imprisonment and up to 14 years for serious offences, personal fines, confiscation of assets, and the CRA's right to lift the corporate veil to collect the tax liability.
